newsHook: Inspired Villages is one of the most active integrated retirement community developers in the UK, building and operating at a point when almost every other operator is telling us capital and planning are the constraint, so operators and investors elsewhere in the sector want to know how the pipeline actually gets delivered.
questions: What is the single biggest thing slowing a retirement community scheme down today, planning or capital, and has that changed in the last two years?
Operators keep hitting the C2 versus C3 use class question. How do you approach it, and what would you change about how councils handle it?
What do you look for in a site before you will take it forward, and what makes you walk away?
The deferred management fee is the part of the model the public understands least. How do you explain it to a buyer, and what would make it less contentious?
What have you changed about how you staff and run a village since opening your first one?
US operators are often held up as the benchmark. What do they do that UK operators have not caught up with yet?
Where does Inspired Villages go from here?

newsHook: McCarthy Stone is the largest developer of retirement housing in the UK and the one whose numbers the rest of the sector reads as the market signal, so operators and investors want to know what the company is seeing in sales, pricing and planning before it shows up in anyone else's results.
questions: What are you seeing in sales rates and pricing right now, and how much of it is the housing market rather than the sector?
How much of a scheme's viability is decided by planning, and where is the system costing the sector most?
Retirement housing and integrated retirement communities get conflated constantly. Where do you draw the line, and does the distinction matter commercially?
What does the resale and buyback side of the model look like in practice, and what would you change about how it is regulated?
Which parts of the operating model have you moved in house, and which are better bought in?
What should a smaller operator learn from the way a company at your scale runs its pipeline?
Where does McCarthy Stone go from here?

newsHook: Richmond Villages runs integrated retirement communities alongside care on the same campuses, which is the model most operators are arguing about right now, so the sector wants to know how the two sides actually work together on one site.
questions: Running a village and care on one campus is the model everyone debates. What works about it commercially and what is harder than it looks?
How do you decide the amenity mix on a new village, and which amenities earn their space?
What does occupancy actually depend on in your experience, location, price, or the community itself?
How do you recruit and keep village managers, which almost every operator tells us is the binding constraint?
What do residents ask for now that they were not asking for five years ago?
What would you tell an operator opening their first village?
Where do Richmond Villages go from here?

newsHook: New Zealand has run the occupation right agreement model for far longer than the UK has run the deferred management fee, and LifeCare Residences operates on both sides of that experience, so UK operators and investors want to know what a mature deferred-fee market teaches the one that is still forming.
questions: The UK is only now settling its deferred fee model. What did New Zealand get right, and what would you warn the UK about?
How does the occupation right agreement work in practice for the operator's cash flow, and how does it compare to what UK operators are doing?
New Zealand's Retirement Villages Act is under review. What would a good outcome look like for operators, and what would a bad one look like?
What does resident demand look like in New Zealand compared with what you see in the UK?
Construction cost and labour have hit every market. How has that changed what you build?
What would you say to a UK operator looking at the New Zealand model and thinking about importing parts of it?
Where does LifeCare Residences go from here?

newsHook: Retirement Villages Group has been building and running UK retirement communities for longer than almost anyone else in the market and is now developing again at scale, so operators want to know what a long view of this sector teaches about the schemes being approved today.
questions: You have seen this sector through several cycles. What is genuinely different about the one we are in now?
What makes a retirement community scheme work financially, and what is the most common way they go wrong?
How do you get a scheme through planning in a system that still does not have a settled category for it?
Where is the capital coming from for the next wave of schemes, and what do those investors want that they did not want before?
What does a village need to offer now to fill, and what has stopped mattering?
What should the sector be lobbying for that it currently is not?
Where does Retirement Villages Group go from here?

personRole: Professor of Management, University of Leicester; President, British Society of Gerontology
newsHook: You are president of the British Society of Gerontology and you have spent your career inside the datasets that actually measure later life, ELSA, SHARE and SLOSH, which puts you in an unusual position: the people who build and run retirement communities are making very large capital bets on what older people want, and you are one of the few people who can say what the evidence supports and what it does not.
questions: ELSA and SHARE have tracked quality of life in later life for decades. What actually moves it, and how much of that can a retirement community realistically supply?

You chair the BSG's Work and Retirement Group. People now retire later and in stages. What does that do to the age at which someone buys into a retirement community, and what should operators be building for?

Your work on health inequalities in later life is stark, and retirement communities are overwhelmingly bought by the better off. Is the sector reaching the people who would benefit most, and what would change that?
Ageing and Globalisation compares how different countries handle later life. Which country's model should UK operators be studying hardest, and what specifically?
Operators sell independence, community and security. Which of those three does the evidence support as improving outcomes, and which is marketing?
What does the research say about the right point to move, and how does that sit with an industry that needs people to move earlier?
What is the question about later life that this industry is not asking itself?

personRole: Co-Founder, Intergenerational England; Programme Director, Intergenerational Music Making
newsHook: Intergenerational England was set up as the first national body working against age segregation, and a retirement community is by definition an age-segregated place, so the people developing and running them have a direct interest in what you have found works when generations are deliberately mixed and what turns out to be tokenism.
questions: Intergenerational England exists to tackle age segregation, and a retirement community is by definition age-segregated. Is the model part of the problem?
What does a genuinely intergenerational scheme look like in practice, as opposed to a nursery visit once a term?
You have run intergenerational music programmes at scale. What separated the ones that worked from the ones that did not?
If an operator wanted to design intergenerational use into a new village from the planning stage, what would you tell them to build in, and what to avoid?
What does it cost, who pays for it, and how would an operator show a board it was worth the money?
Where are the planning and regulatory obstacles to mixing ages on one site in England?
Which scheme or operator in England is doing this best right now, and what are they doing that the others are not?

personRole: ENRICH Cymru Research Manager, School of Health and Social Care, Swansea University
newsHook: Loneliness in later life is the thing retirement communities implicitly sell against, and you have spent your career measuring it, including the work classifying distinct patterns of loneliness and isolation and the finding that loneliness can act as a biographical disruption, so operators want to know whether moving into a community actually does what they say it does.
questions: Your work identified distinct patterns of loneliness and isolation in later life rather than one condition. What are they, and does moving into a retirement community help all of them equally?
You have described loneliness as a biographical disruption. Is moving into a village itself a disruption of that kind, and what should an operator do in the first six months?
Retirement communities sell community. What does the evidence say about whether living among other older people actually reduces loneliness?
You have looked at communication technology and isolation. What should an operator actually install or run, and what is wasted money?
You sit on the Welsh Government loneliness strategy board. What is policy now asking of housing providers, and is retirement housing inside that conversation or outside it?
If you were an operator who genuinely wanted to know whether your community was working, what would you measure?
What does the research say about the resident who stays lonely inside a busy community, and what can be done for them?

personRole: Professor of Work and Employment, University of Leicester; Director, Centre for Research into the Older Workforce
newsHook: Two things this sector is struggling with sit inside your work: people are retiring later and in stages, which moves the age at which anyone buys into a retirement community, and operators consistently name recruiting and keeping village managers as their binding constraint while you have spent years on what makes work attractive to older people.
questions: Phased retirement is replacing the cliff edge. What does that do to when people move into a retirement community, and what do they need from one if they are still working?

You have written good practice guides for employers on making work attractive to older workers. Retirement village operators say recruiting and keeping village managers is their hardest problem. What should they be doing differently?
Second Mission follows people who change career after fifty. Are retirement housing and care a realistic destination for them, and how would the sector attract them?
Is there a case for operators recruiting staff from the same age group as their residents, and what does the evidence say about how that works in customer-facing roles?
If people are working into their seventies, does the core proposition of a retirement community have to change?
Which employers are genuinely good at intergenerational teams, and what do they do that a village operator could copy?
What single change to policy or practice would most help an ageing workforce, and does it reach this sector at all?
